entry.title: ESBMC reads Kani’s GOTO: a second engine for Rust standard-library proofs

link.title: ESBMC reads Kani’s GOTO: a second engine for Rust standard-library proofs

entry.content:
Safe Rust eliminates data races, dangling references and out of bounds accesses, provided the unsafe code beneath it plays its part. A fair bit of that unsafe code is in the standard library. Vec, String, slice, NonNull and the integer types all wrap raw pointer arithmetic, uninitialised memory and compiler intrinsics up with safe APIs and every Rust program assumes those wrappers are correct. A single missing bounds check in core is a bug in every program that uses it.

The Verifying the Rust Standard Library challenge (run by AWS with the support of the Rust Foundation) takes that trust and turns it into proof obligations [1]. The repo is a fork of the Rust library with verification harnesses side by side with the code under scrutiny and CI runs all the approved tools on every PR. ESBMC [2] is one of the five tools listed in the README as accepted (along with Kani, Flux, KMIR and VeriFast). ESBMC doesn’t parse Rust at all. It verifies the same harnesses that Kani does, by reading the CBMC GOTO binaries that Kani produces.

This is all about the change that made that route viable. Prior to this year there was a separate program (goto-transcoder) that would take Kani’s output and convert it into ESBMC’s own GOTO format. Since ESBMC v8.4 we’ve had esbmc --binary which can read Kani’s CBMC binaries directly. The CI for the challenge stopped invoking the transcoder in October (verify-rust-std#710) and removed the name last week (#779). On a sweep of all 1,888 harnesses in the repo, the ESBMC master branch now agrees with Kani on 1,784 of them (94.5%) with zero false alarms and zero missed bugs, at 900s and 15 GB per harness. The rest of this post goes into how we got there, what that figure actually means and what it doesn’t.

Figure 1. Kani compiles each harness down to a CBMC GOTO binary. CBMC is Kani’s own back end. ESBMC used to require the goto-transcoder in between (dashed) but since v8.4 it just reads the binary itself.

A harness from the standard library

Here’s one of the harnesses that the challenge’s ESBMC job checks. The integer types in core have unchecked_mul which will multiply without any overflow check and is undefined behavior if the result overflows. A requires clause is provided to indicate when a call is safe (library/core/src/num/int_macros.rs):

#[requires(!self.overflowing_mul(rhs).1)]
pub const unsafe fn unchecked_mul(self, rhs: Self) -> Self {

and a macro in library/core/src/num/mod.rs generates one harness per integer type:

#[kani::proof_for_contract($type::$method)]
pub fn $harness_name() {
    let num1: $type = kani::any::<$type>();
    let num2: $type = kani::any::<$type>();
    unsafe {
        num1.$method(num2);
    }
}

kani::any makes both operands nondeterministic so the harness covers every pair of values. proof_for_contract tells Kani to assume the requires clause and then check that the body doesn’t panic, doesn’t have any arithmetic overflow and doesn’t have any undefined behavior that Kani models. The 1,888 harnesses in the repo are all of this form: 1,236 are contract harnesses of this type and 652 are plain #[kani::proof] harnesses.

Where Kani’s work ends and a back end begins

Kani is a Rust model checker built on top of CBMC. It has its own compiler (kani-compiler) which hooks into rustc, takes the program after it’s been lowered to MIR (rustc’s mid-level IR) and translates that into a GOTO program (CBMC’s intermediate language of assignments, guarded jumps, function calls, assumptions and assertions). Kani then runs goto-instrument and CBMC on that program and interprets the report that CBMC produces.

Every Rust-specific decision (the layout of an enum, where each overflow check goes etc) has been made by the time the GOTO binary is written. The back end just has to answer the question “can any assertion fail?” That’s where ESBMC comes in. Kani with --keep-temps --only-codegen stops after codegen and produces one .out file per harness. A second engine that reads those files inherits Kani’s Rust semantics and then adds its own search. ESBMC encodes the program into SMT (Bitwuzla is the default solver) rather than SAT and offers k-induction and incremental BMC on top of plain bounded model checking. If two engines disagree on the same binary then one of them has a bug and the binary is a ready made reproducer.

The first integration: translate, then verify

One of us (Rafael) built the first bridge in 2024. goto-transcoder is a Rust program which takes a CBMC GOTO binary and outputs the same program in ESBMC’s GOTO format. The two formats are quite distant from each other despite sharing a common ancestry (ESBMC was originally a fork of CBMC). The encoding of a number is different too: CBMC writes varint words (7 bits per byte) and ESBMC writes big-endian 32-bit words. In Jan 2025 the challenge’s CI started off running ESBMC via the transcoder on the checked_unchecked_* contracts (verify-rust-std#236). The job would take each .out, link it to a prebuilt library.goto with ESBMC’s C library and entry point and then run ESBMC on the result.

It worked, but it introduced a third program between Kani and the verdict with its own release cycle. Kani’s output changes as Kani evolves and every change had to be picked up by the transcoder and ESBMC in turn. By October 2026 that coupling had broken with ESBMC 7.10 segfaulting on the transcoder’s output for every contract built by Kani main (verify-rust-std#710).

Reading the binary in ESBMC

The direct reader arrived as esbmc#5291 in June 2026 and shipped with v8.4. It’s essentially the same design as the transcoder, just running inside ESBMC.

  1. goto_binary_reader looks at the magic bytes. 0x7f 'G' 'B' 'F' takes you down the CBMC path, plain GBF is the native one.
  2. read_cbmc_goto_object.cpp deals with decoding the varint stream, the shared string and shared subtree references and the symbol and function tables. It supports format version 6.
  3. cbmc_adapter.cpp takes CBMC’s expressions and type conventions and converts them into ESBMC’s, renumbers the jump targets and resolves the struct tags.
  4. ESBMC compiles a minimal boilerplate C file via its own front-end to produce what the library.goto used to supply (the C library models and the __ESBMC_main entry wrapper) and then links it in the same process.
  5. The entry wrapper is pointed at CBMC’s __CPROVER__start or at the harness named by --function.

From there it goes through ESBMC’s normal pipeline: GOTO processing, symbolic execution, SMT encoding, solving. The hello world harness from Kani’s tutorial runs as:

esbmc --binary test__RNvCsjN3sjT3oKaE_4test4main.out --function _RNvCsjN3sjT3oKaE_4test4main

and ESBMC prints CBMC goto-binary detected: linking ESBMC additions automatically prior to it starting. No library.goto is involved.

Why reading the binary directly matters

Removing a conversion step sounds like plumbing. The engineering record of the reader is quite clear on this point: the difficult bit about consuming another tool’s intermediate language is the meaning of the program, the bytes are the easy bit. A reader that correctly decodes every byte can still give the wrong answer and indeed several of the early bugs did just that.

  • Instruction kinds. ESBMC and CBMC number their GOTO instruction kinds identically up to 18 and then diverge at 19 (CBMC has INCOMPLETE_GOTO, ESBMC has THROW_DECL). esbmc#5717 replaced the implicit numeric match with an explicit table and rejects the kinds that ESBMC models differently (START_THREAD, END_THREAD) with a named diagnostic.
  • Entry point. Prior to esbmc#5719 the synthesized __ESBMC_main would have called the boilerplate’s empty main rather than the harness. ESBMC would verify an empty program and could therefore report VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL on a harness whose assertion does in fact fail.
  • Memory predicates. CBMC’s __CPROVER_r_ok, w_ok and rw_ok were initially set to constant true, so ESBMC proved __CPROVER_r_ok(malloc(8), 16), which CBMC of course refutes. esbmc#7411 gave them a proper encoding.
  • Wide constants. The adapter was padding out every converted constant to 32 bits in exactly the same way as the reference converter did, so x == -5000000000LL would read x as a positive 32 bit value and ESBMC would report a false FAILED. esbmc#5916 made the conversion respect the width of the constant.

That last bug was part of the port. The transcoder had it too. Moving the reader into ESBMC meant that every such convention was now right next to the code that depended on it, with a fix and a regression test landing in the same pull request. The regression/goto-transcoder directory in ESBMC (despite the name) now contains 385 tests that all load a CBMC binary. At least 60 of those are Kani written.

The second reason is information that a converter is likely to lose. CBMC attaches a property class to each assertion, goto-cc and Kani write loop invariants on the loop back edges, and Kani’s helper functions all have the __KANI_ prefix. A reader inside ESBMC sees all of that and can act on it. The converter has to pass all that information through to the second format and each one it loses is going to change what ESBMC is asked to verify.

Making ESBMC behave like a Kani back end

Reading the binary is necessary but not sufficient. Kani’s driver does the interpretation of CBMC’s raw output and ESBMC has to do the same interpretation in order to give the same answer. Most of the work this autumn was down in that area.

Reachability and cover checks. Kani inserts assertions which are intended to fail. A reachability_check fails if its location is reachable and a cover fails if its condition can be satisfied. Kani treats both as information rather than as bugs. After the kani#5093 change every contract harness had one and every contract failed under ESBMC (esbmc#10875). ESBMC v8.6 added --ignore-property-class which removes those assertions and esbmc#10877 added --report-property-class which omits them from the verdict and just reports them afterwards as REACHABLE, UNREACHABLE, SATISFIED or UNSATISFIABLE.

Kani’s assumptions. Kani runs CBMC with --no-malloc-may-fail. ESBMC’s default is to allow malloc to return NULL which gave us two false alarms (check_vecdeque_swap and verify_swap_remove). Since esbmc#10975, if ESBMC sees a symbol called __KANI_... in a CBMC binary it assumes malloc and realloc both succeed. esbmc#10902 likewise stopped ESBMC from adding an alignment check that CBMC doesn’t make, which was the reason Kani’s unaligned-load harnesses were failing.

A default strategy. Lots of harnesses have loops with no unwinding bound. Plain BMC just keeps unrolling them and in our very first full sweep 134 harnesses ran out of memory that way. esbmc#10942 by default has ESBMC verify a Kani binary with --k-induction --unlimited-k-steps --max-inductive-step 3 unless a strategy or bound is specified on the command line. We ran the four strategies on the same 1,888 harnesses in the first instance (master 4757f8a6bd, 900s, 15 GB): plain BMC agreed with Kani on 1,690, k-induction on 1,716, incremental BMC on 1,707 and IC3/PDR (--ts-pdr) on 1,700. PDR reported 7 harnesses as safe that Kani expects to be unsafe. k-induction had the most agreements and reported none of those harnesses as safe so it became the default.

Pointer and memory modeling. The rest is just standard model checker work. Rust’s core exercises the model checker a lot harder than most C code really does: pointers through unions and byte-level reinterprets (esbmc#10948, #10969, #11012), r_ok ranges near 263 (#10943) and objects that absolutely must not cross 263 (#10922). One of the issues in that area actually demonstrates the value of a second engine. Three false alarms in the sweep (check_bytes, check_invariant, check_u64_fmt) all traced back to esbmc#10965. When symbolic execution can’t propagate a struct member then a copy of the struct will have a read of its source and the copy’s pointer will then follow the source’s later value. On a 15 line C program that same defect leads to a false proof which CBMC refutes on the same binary. esbmc#10969 fixed both.

ESBMC in the challenge’s CI

The challenge runs ESBMC in its own workflow (esbmc.yml). It has two steps: scripts/run-kani.sh --kani-args --keep-temps --only-codegen to build the GOTO binaries and scripts/run-esbmc.sh which downloads a pinned ESBMC release and then runs it for each of the selected harnesses.

esbmc --binary <harness>.out --function <harness> \
    --ignore-property-class reachability_check --ignore-property-class cover

verify-rust-std#710 switched to the direct reader in October. #779 (merged 20th November) pinned v8.7, added the property class options and renamed the workflow, script and documentation from goto-transcoder to ESBMC.

What the CI actually checks is very narrow. The workflow picks up checked_unchecked.*.out which today matches four contracts (unchecked_mul for i8, u8, i16 and u16). On the last run on main (Nov 21 ESBMC 8.7.0, Bitwuzla 0.9.0) all four reported VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL. That’s the full extent of the ESBMC results in the CI challenge. A PR to move the job to v8.8 (which has the k-induction and malloc defaults) is open (verify-rust-std#789).

Measuring the whole repository

To get a sense of just how far the route goes beyond those four contracts we ran ESBMC on every harness in the repository (outside of the challenge CI). The setup was:

  • Harnesses: all 1,888 in verify-rust-std at the merge of #766, compiled by the Kani commit that the CI pins to (53cb531). For 1,772 of them Kani expects a success, for the other 116 Kani expects a failing check (e.g. the harness is marked should_panic).
  • Reference: Kani’s own CI run on the same commit confirms all 1,888 as expected. “Agree” means ESBMC’s verdict matches Kani’s expectation. A false alarm is a FAILED when Kani expects it to succeed. A missed bug is a SUCCESSFUL when Kani expects it to fail.
  • Limits: 900s and 15GB per harness, one core, under BenchExec on an AWS r7a.16xlarge instance, ESBMC built from master.
ESBMC Configuration Agree (n = 1,888) False alarm Missed bug Timeout Out of memory
master 4757f8a6bd plain BMC 1,690 (89.5%) 12 0 52 134
master 03233ba208 default for Kani binaries (k-induction) 1,784 (94.5%) 0 0 103 1
master 03233ba208 default plus --loop-invariant 1,780 (94.3%) 0 0 106 0
master 03233ba208 --parallel-solving --multi-property, harness bounds as --unwindset, 4 cores 1,745 (92.4%) 0 0 30 113

Row 1 is from 22nd Nov, the other three from 24th Nov. In the default config the 23 harnesses that have a #[kani::unwind] bound are all running with that bound under plain BMC (a bound on the command line turns off the k-induction default). There are two UNKNOWNs to complete the --loop-invariant row. For an earlier reference point we reported last week that ESBMC v8.7, under much tighter constraints of 60s and 4 GB, agreed with Kani on 79.3% of the same 1,888 harnesses (the rest were using CBMC GOTO features that v8.7 didn’t support). Those constraints are very different from those in the table so the figure is not directly comparable.

Three readings follow from the table and one claim doesn’t.

Wrong answers are extremely rare and none remain in this corpus. No config on 03233ba208 has a false alarm or a missed bug and none of the twelve harnesses that false-alarmed under plain BMC on 4757f8a6bd still do. The fixes described above (including #10969) are in between the two commits.

What’s left is cost, not unsupported features. In the default configuration every one of the 1,888 binaries loads and every harness ESBMC doesn’t decide stopped at a resource limit (103 timeouts, one memory out). Kani doesn’t have that problem on those harnesses. On the challenge CI runners Kani’s CBMC verifies all 103 with a median of 8.7s and a max of 293s (non_null_check_write_unaligned_u128). The machines are different so the comparison is just indicative but the direction is clear: on those harnesses CBMC’s SAT encoding is faster than ESBMC’s current encoding.

Spending more cores on the parallel solving didn’t help at all – parallel solving still didn’t recover any harnesses. In fact 73 of the former timeouts and 39 harnesses that had agreed just ran out of memory instead. That’s consistent with the way that option was keeping one solver per claim alive at once. Master has now bounded it with a worker pool (esbmc#11047) and we’re re-running that config to see the effect.

What the table doesn’t show is that ESBMC finds bugs that Kani misses. All the harnesses in the repository already pass under Kani so this is a measure of how much of Kani’s ground the second engine covers and how often the two engines disagree. It’s a per harness comparison rather than a per property comparison and it’s using ESBMC’s master branch rather than a release. v8.8 has the k-induction and malloc defaults in it but not #10969 or #11012.

A harder case: float-to-decimal conversion

By construction every harness in the repo is one that Kani can finish. Challenge 28 (safety proofs for the float-to-decimal code in core::num::flt2dec) is a better test of what a second engine might be able to contribute. The harnesses so far have either stubbed or assumed away the arithmetic in the Grisu and Dragon digit loops. We did write a plan to run the unstubbed loops through ESBMC and set a gate for it: the unstubbed Grisu harnesses had to be in budget.

They didn’t. On ESBMC v8.8, not a single unstubbed Grisu harness completed, even at 3600s (four times the sweep budget). Splitting the f64 shortest mode harness into one run per claim (900s each, with round_and_weed’s loop bounded at 10) managed 100 of the 111 claims (including all of the Fp::mul overflow checks and the digit bound q < 10 that the submitted solutions assume). The 11 that timed out are the buf[i] index check, one comparison and nine of the overflow checks on the error bounded arithmetic in the digit loop. We recorded that as a failed gate. In the process it led to a model of memset with a symbolic offset or length (esbmc#11018) and the per-claim results reduce the open part of the problem to just a handful of claims which would require loop invariants.

What ESBMC does not support yet

These are different categories and to mix them would be to misrepresent where ESBMC actually stands.

CBMC and Kani GOTO features ESBMC does not handle. Reader accepts GOTO format version 6 only. It declines (with an error rather than a wrong verdict) SIMD operations, setjmp, va_start and __CPROVER_DYNAMIC_OBJECT as well as __CPROVER_havoc_object on a pointer value and __CPROVER_array_set on arrays that are not whole objects. For contracts is_fresh allocates and writes through but does not check separation between pointers. All of these are from the CPROVER support roadmap (last reviewed October 1) and none of them appear in the default sweep above.

Loop and frame contracts. esbmc#11017 applies the loop invariants that goto-cc and Kani store in the binary (via --loop-invariant and related options). It has no effect on Kani at this stage: Kani simply lowers #[kani::loop_invariant(...)] to a call of a generated closure and the reader will ignore any invariant that has a side effect. That will impact all 13 verify-rust-std harnesses that have a loop contract (esbmc#11051, open). ESBMC also never sees any modifies clauses as --only-codegen stops before goto-instrument, the step that turns them into checks.

Options which don’t work on Kani binaries. With --ir (unbounded integers) ESBMC aborts on Kani binaries which do a struct to integer cast (which NonNull::dangling() does) (esbmc#11023, open). The default bit-vector encoding works with the same binaries.

Resource limits. The 104 harnesses without a verdict in the default sweep ran out of time or memory. One known culprit is memcpy with a symbolic length at a symbolic offset which still falls back to a byte loop that unwinds to the bound (esbmc#11026, open).

What comes next

  • Run more of the repo in the challenge’s CI. The job currently checks four contracts with v8.7. The first step is to move to v8.8 (#789) but the one that actually makes a difference is to broaden the scope beyond checked_unchecked.
  • Close 104. Profile the timeouts by module (starting with the symbolic memcpy and the non_null_check_*_unaligned family) and see if #11047 brings back the harnesses that --parallel-solving lost due to memory.
  • Kani loop contracts. Evaluate the closure call where the invariant is checked (#11051) so that --loop-invariant gets to the 13 harnesses that carry one.
  • Compare per property. Agreement on a verdict can hide disagreement on individual checks. --multi-property with --report-property-class gives the per-check report needed to compare against Kani claim by claim.

Reading the binary directly changes what ESBMC can be in this ecosystem. Before, it was a tool that verified a translation of Kani’s output, and the translation could break with any Kani release. Now it reads the same binary CBMC reads, applies the same assumptions Kani makes, and runs a different solver stack and different proof strategies over it. On the 1,888 harnesses we measured, that second engine agrees with the first on 94.5% and never contradicts it. Where the two part ways, a disagreement points to a bug in one of them and comes with a binary that reproduces it. The open question is whether ESBMC can prove harnesses Kani cannot. Challenge 28 says not yet, for unstubbed Grisu, and the per-claim results there show where to look next.

Join us

We are looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators interested in Rust verification, model checking and SMT. ESBMC is open source, and the CBMC reader, its 385 regression tests and the roadmap documents are in ESBMC master. If this interests you, email Lucas Cordeiro with a short note on what you would like to work on, or talk to the group first on our public Zulip chat.

References

  • [1] B. Cook et al., “Verifying the Rust Standard Library,” in NASA Formal Methods (NFM 2026), in Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16622. Springer, 2026, pp. 415–435. doi: 10.1007/978-3-032-28079-4_19. DOI
  • [2] P. V. Dantas, L. C. Cordeiro, and W. S. S. Júnior, “ESBMC: A Survey of Its Evolution, Integration, and Future Directions in Formal Software Verification,” CoRR, vol. abs/2605.26169, 2026, doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2605.26169. DOI

author.name: Lucas C. Cordeiro and Rafael Sá Menezes

entry.summary: ESBMC now verifies the CBMC GOTO binaries that Kani generates for the Rust proof harnesses, with no conversion step in between. We explain what's changed, why it's important to be reading the binary directly and what a sweep over all 1,888 verify-rust-std harnesses does and doesn't show.

entry.title: Translating ESBMC programs into Lean: what a second prover adds

link.title: Translating ESBMC programs into Lean: what a second prover adds

entry.content:
A model checker reports one of three verdicts: safe, unsafe or unknown. ESBMC prints them as VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL, VERIFICATION FAILED and VERIFICATION UNKNOWN. An unsafe verdict is easy to validate, because it comes with a counterexample that can be replayed against the program. A safe verdict is harder. It is the output of a parser, a symbolic execution engine, a simplifier, an SMT encoding and a solver working in sequence, and a defect in any of them can make an incorrect program look safe. Our last post ended by asking who checks the checker. ESBMC already writes verification witnesses that other teams’ validators check in SV-COMP, but a validator re-verifies the witness with its own engine, and that engine is trusted in turn.

ESBMC is the SMT-based model checker that we develop [1]. Its front ends for C, C++, Python and Solidity all produce the same intermediate language, the GOTO program. A new option, --goto2lean, prints that program as Lean 4 definitions, together with a theorem stating that no assertion fails. Lean is a proof assistant: a proof counts only once Lean’s kernel, a small checker, has accepted it. The kernel checks the finished proof independently of the automation that built it, so a bug in that automation can make a proof fail but cannot make Lean accept a false theorem. So far the new option --goto2lean handles Booleans and integers, if/else, loops, calls to non-recursive functions, and quantifiers in assertions. It rejects arrays and pointers.

The two provers help each other in both directions. When ESBMC cannot finish a proof, Lean sometimes can, and Lean’s proof shows which reasoning steps ESBMC was missing; we wrote some of those steps back into the C program and ESBMC finished. Lean, in turn, depends on a loop invariant that someone has to supply, and ESBMC rejects a wrong one within seconds, with a concrete state that shows what is missing. And if the two disagree on a program, at least one of them has a bug, which is the check our last post asked for. This work even helped us find a bug in ESBMC (fixed in #10576): an invalid simplification in unbounded-integer mode (--ir), where arithmetic on constants still wrapped at 32 bits.

Figure 1. Two routes from the same GOTO program. Both start after the front end. The dashed arrows are the exchanges this post describes: Lean’s proof steps become hints for ESBMC (1), and ESBMC rejects wrong invariants before Lean tries them (2). When the two results disagree, one of the provers has a bug.

Note that all results below were measured locally, with ESBMC’s development version and Lean 4.35.0.

A loop that ESBMC cannot finish

Our first example is a loop that adds up the first n cubes and the first n whole numbers, then asserts Nicomachus’s theorem: the sum of the cubes equals the square of the sum, \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i^3 = \left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i\right)^2\). For n = 4, 0 + 1 + 8 + 27 = 36 = (0 + 1 + 2 + 3)2.

unsigned nondet_uint(void);
int main(void) {
  unsigned n = nondet_uint();
  unsigned s = 0, c = 0, i = 0;
  while (i < n) {
    s = s + i;
    c = c + i * i * i;
    i = i + 1;
  }
  __ESBMC_assert(c == s * s, "Nicomachus");
  return 0;
}

The program uses 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so large values wrap around. Nicomachus’s theorem survives that. It is an equation built from additions and multiplications, both sides wrap in the same way, and the assertion holds for every n.

Proving something about a loop for every n needs a loop invariant: a predicate that is true before the loop and stays true after each iteration. ESBMC does not find one here by itself, and plain k-induction answers VERIFICATION UNKNOWN. So we supplied one with __ESBMC_loop_invariant: 2 * s == i * (i - 1), c == s * s and i <= n. The hard part is the middle fact. ESBMC has to show that if c equals s * s before an iteration, then c + i * i * i equals (s + i) * (s + i) after it. It passes that question to an SMT solver, which handles 32-bit arithmetic by turning every multiplication into a circuit of logic gates and searching the circuit for a counterexample. Cubing a 32-bit number gives a large circuit. Neither of the two solvers we tried, Z3 and Bitwuzla, answered within five minutes.

esbmc ucubes.c --goto2lean produces this Lean file instead:

def main_loop1 (n : BitVec 32) (s : BitVec 32) (c : BitVec 32) (i : BitVec 32)
    (post : BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → Prop)
    (ret : BitVec 32 → Prop) : Prop :=
  (¬(i < n) →
    post n s c i) ∧
  ((i < n) →
  let s := (s + i);
  let c := (c + ((i * i) * i));
  let i := (i + (1#32));
  main_loop1 n s c i post ret)
coinductive_fixpoint

def main (post : BitVec 32 → Prop) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : BitVec 32,
  let s := (0#32);
  let c := (0#32);
  let i := (0#32);
  main_loop1 n s c i (fun (n : BitVec 32) (s : BitVec 32) (c : BitVec 32) (i : BitVec 32) =>
    -- Nicomachus
    (c = (s * s)) ∧ (
    post (0#32))) post

theorem main_safe : Prog.main (fun _ => True) := by
  -- Not closed automatically: each loop needs an invariant (apply Prog.<loop>.coinduct).
  sorry

Listing 1. The Lean that --goto2lean generates for the loop, with the namespace and one renaming line removed. sorry is Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof.

Listing 1 is the inductive version of the program. The while loop is gone; in its place is main_loop1, a definition that refers to itself. Read it as a statement about one visit to the loop head with the current values of n, s, c and i. If i < n is false, the loop exits and the final check c = s * s must hold. Otherwise the body runs once, giving new values of s, c and i, and the same statement must hold again for those values, which is the self-reference. main makes the first visit, with s, c and i at zero and n arbitrary (the ∀). The rest of the file follows one pattern: a nondeterministic value becomes ∀, an __ESBMC_assume becomes →, and an assertion becomes ∧. One keyword is new: coinductive_fixpoint allows the loop to run forever. A run that never exits never reaches the assertion, so the theorem only constrains runs that terminate.

From that definition Lean derives a proof rule, Prog.main_loop1.coinduct. To use it, you give a property of the loop variables. You then show that it holds at the first visit, and that whenever it holds at the loop head, the statement above holds with the property in place of the self-reference. That property is the loop invariant, and the rule is the loop-invariant rule of Hoare logic. Lean derives it from the definition, so the rule itself does not have to be trusted. Replacing sorry with the invariant we gave ESBMC, plus one line of automation, completes the proof:

theorem main_safe : Prog.main (fun _ => True) := by
  simp only [Prog.main]
  intro n
  apply Prog.main_loop1.coinduct n _ _
    (fun s c i => 2#32 * s = i * (i - 1#32) ∧ c = s * s ∧ i ≤ n)
  all_goals grind

Listing 2. The proof that replaces sorry. Lean checks it in 1.7 seconds.

The apply ... coinduct line leaves three goals: the invariant holds before the loop, it survives one iteration, and on exit it implies the assertion. all_goals grind sends each of them to grind, Lean’s general-purpose automation, the hammer you try before writing a proof by hand. So the only part a person writes is the invariant, the same one we gave ESBMC. Our first version of the proof handled each goal by hand, using grind for the step and bv_omega (Lean’s tactic for linear bit-vector arithmetic) for the bounds. Lean’s try? command, which searches for a tactic that closes the current goal, suggested grind for the goals we tried it on, and a single all_goals grind then closed all three. The translator could emit these lines whenever the program carries an __ESBMC_loop_invariant; it does not do so yet.

Part of what grind does is algebra. On the step, it expands (s + i) * (s + i), uses 2 * s = i * (i - 1) to rewrite the result, and finds that both sides are the same polynomial, as you would on paper. It never builds a circuit, so the cube costs it no more than a sum. The gain comes from the algebra, not from Lean as such. When we replaced grind with bv_decide, the Lean tactic that does build a circuit and call a SAT solver, it timed out too.

What ESBMC can learn from Lean’s proof

Lean finished the proof, but ESBMC is the tool people run on their code, so we asked what Lean’s proof could teach it. The proof does three things that ESBMC’s single query to the solver does not. Lean proves the start, the step and the exit as separate goals. At the exit it has to conclude i = n from i ≤ n and ¬(i < n), which our hand-written version did in one line (have : i = n := by bv_omega; subst this). And on the step, grind uses the invariant’s equations as rewrite rules. We tested each move by writing it back into the C program.

Hints and separate goals. We copied grind’s algebra into the loop body as four __ESBMC_assume statements: the expansion of (s + i) * (s + i), the regrouping of 2 * s * i, the substitution of i * (i - 1) for 2 * s, and the expansion of i * (i - 1) * i + i * i. Each holds for every 32-bit value. ESBMC proves the two expansions in under a second each, as separate programs. The regrouping needs no proof: C’s * associates to the left, so 2 * s * i already means (2 * s) * i, and ESBMC’s simplifier removes this hint before the solver sees it. The substitution is congruence: equal values multiplied by the same i stay equal. Over plain variables ESBMC proves it in under a second, but with the products written in, neither Z3 nor Bitwuzla proves it within 300 seconds, while Lean closes it with rw [h]. We then ran ESBMC with --multi-property, which sends each claim to the solver on its own, the way Lean splits its proof into goals. Z3 proves the 32-bit program in 6.0 seconds:

unsigned nondet_uint(void);
int main(void) {
  unsigned n = nondet_uint();
  unsigned s = 0, c = 0, i = 0;
  __ESBMC_loop_invariant(2 * s == i * (i - 1) && c == s * s && i <= n);
  while (i < n) {
    __ESBMC_assume((s + i) * (s + i) == s * s + 2 * s * i + i * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(2 * s * i == (2 * s) * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(2 * s != i * (i - 1) || (2 * s) * i == (i * (i - 1)) * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(i * (i - 1) * i + i * i == i * i * i);
    s = s + i;
    c = c + i * i * i;
    i = i + 1;
  }
  __ESBMC_assert(c == s * s, "Nicomachus");
  return 0;
}

Listing 3. The 32-bit Nicomachus program with grind’s steps written in. esbmc --loop-invariant-check --multi-property --z3 reports VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL in 6.0 seconds.

Each half fails without the other, for different reasons. Without the hints, the step times out even on its own. Our reading is that the solver would have to discover intermediate terms such as (2 * s) * i inside the multiplier circuits. The hints name those terms and say how they relate, so the step becomes a chain of equalities: (s + i)2 = s2 + (2s)·i + i2 = s2 + i(i − 1)·i + i2 = s2 + i3 = c + i3. Given the hints, Z3 proves the step in 4.7 seconds.

Without --multi-property, ESBMC puts all claims into one query, and there the hints looked useless: neither solver answered in 300 seconds. We traced that to the exit claim, which checks that the invariant implies the assertion once the loop ends. Checked by itself, the exit claim follows directly from the invariant, and Z3 proves it in under a millisecond. The start and the step, checked together in one query without the exit claim, prove in 2.6 seconds. Put all three in one query and Z3 times out. We do not yet know why the combination is so much harder than its parts. Bitwuzla timed out in every configuration we tried, so these results hold for Z3 only.

The 32-bit Gauss loop, which keeps only s and asserts 2 * s == n * (n - 1), broke where we least expected it. With its invariant, both solvers stall on the exit claim: from 2 * s == i * (i - 1), i <= n and !(i < n), conclude 2 * s == n * (n - 1). Written with i == n in place of the two inequalities, the same claim takes 0.46 seconds in both solvers. The solvers never derive the equality and substitute it. They compare two 32-bit multipliers bit by bit, and Lean’s proof avoids that with one line. With __ESBMC_assert(i == n, ...) after the loop and --multi-property, Z3 proves the whole Gauss program in 0.57 seconds. Either change alone leaves it without a verdict.

Two of these moves could become ESBMC heuristics. The exit equality is cheap and local: when an invariant contains i <= n and the loop exits on !(i < n), ESBMC can add i == n and substitute it before checking what follows. Solving the claims of an invariant separately is already an option and could be the default under --loop-invariant-check. The rewriting is harder. As a claim of its own, the identity behind grind’s step, (s + i)2 − (c + i3) = (s2 − c) + i·(2s − i(i − 1)), proves in 0.45 seconds in both solvers, but adding it as a fact to the step does not help. Bitwuzla’s built-in abstraction of multiplication, which by default starts at 33 bits, did not help either when we lowered it to 32 bits on ESBMC’s formulas. What the solvers lack is the use of an equation between products as a rewrite rule. That needs a pass in ESBMC that normalizes polynomials and substitutes the invariant’s equations before the formula reaches the solver. We have not built it; Listing 3 does its job by hand.

What Lean can get from ESBMC

Lean’s proof stands or falls with the invariant, and whoever proposes invariants, a person or a language model, gets some of them wrong. Telling why an invariant is wrong is what ESBMC does well and Lean does not.

So we put ESBMC in front of Lean, in a short shell script. It takes a list of candidate invariants, each written once in C and once in Lean. For each candidate it runs esbmc --loop-invariant-check --multi-property with a 30-second budget. If ESBMC refutes the candidate, the script prints the failing claim and ESBMC’s state. When ESBMC has no verdict, the script writes the proof of Listing 2 with the candidate in place of the invariant and runs Lean on it. We gave it three wrong candidates for the 32-bit Nicomachus loop, and also ran Lean on each of them directly:

Candidate invariant ESBMC Lean, all_goals grind
c == s * s && i <= n rejected in 0.45 s: the step fails at a given state fails in 1.9 s, 1,162 lines of diagnostics
2 * s == i * (i + 1) && c == s * s && i <= n rejected in 0.42 s: the step fails at a given state fails in 1.8 s, 514 lines
4 * c == i * i * (i - 1) * (i - 1) && 2 * s == i * (i - 1) && i <= n rejected in 10.8 s: too weak for the assertion, at a given state fails in 1.9 s, 923 lines

Each rejection comes with a reason. For the first candidate, ESBMC’s state has i = 255 and s = 67372036, so 2 * s is 134744072 while i * (i - 1) is 64770: nothing in the invariant ties s to i, and one more iteration breaks c == s * s. The third candidate is the closed form of the sum of cubes, which an engineer or a model could well propose, and it is true over the integers. Over 32-bit words, 4 * c == (2 * s) * (2 * s) fixes c only up to multiples of 230. ESBMC’s state on exit, s = 229 and c = 230, satisfies the invariant, while s * s wraps to 0 and the assertion fails. ESBMC reports this as UNKNOWN, invariant too weak, because the state need not be reachable in the real program; for screening, it rules the candidate out all the same.

Lean fails on all three as well, and about as fast, but a failed grind is not a rejection. It can mean that the invariant is wrong or only that grind needs help, and its diagnostics do not say which. They include an assignment for the linear part of the problem, but there each product is a free unknown: for the third candidate, grind sets s to 2147483648 and, independently, the square of s to 1. That is not a state of the program.

A rejection from ESBMC does not have to be taken on trust either. Lean checks ESBMC’s state for the third candidate by evaluation, with decide, in 1.5 seconds: the invariant holds, the loop has exited, and c ≠ s * s.

What comes next

  • Heuristics learned from Lean’s proofs. The exit equality and per-claim solving are small changes to ESBMC, and we plan to try them first. The larger one is the rewriting pass that Listing 3 does by hand: normalize polynomials and substitute the invariant’s equations before the formula reaches the solver.
  • Proof scripts from the translator. When the program carries an __ESBMC_loop_invariant, --goto2lean could emit the apply and all_goals grind lines of Listing 2 instead of sorry, so that a proof like this one needs no Lean from the user.
  • Invariants from models, screened by ESBMC. The screening script is the first piece. Next we connect it to a language model that proposes the candidates [2], so that ESBMC discards the wrong ones and Lean proves the rest.
  • Prove the translator. Neither route checks --goto2lean itself. Rafael’s PhD thesis [3] gives GOTO a formal semantics, partly mechanized in Isabelle; carried over to Lean, it would let us prove the translator correct and state when an ESBMC pass preserves a program’s meaning.

Join us

We are looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators interested in these problems: formal methods, program analysis and interactive theorem proving. ESBMC is open source, and the translator, its regression tests and its documentation are in ESBMC master. If this interests you, email Lucas Cordeiro with a short note on what you would like to work on, or talk to the group first on our public Zulip chat.

author.name: Lucas C. Cordeiro and Rafael Sá Menezes

entry.summary: ESBMC can now translate its GOTO programs into Lean 4. We ran both provers on the same programs to see what each can take from the other, and what a disagreement between them tells us.

entry.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

link.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

entry.content:
A language model can produce a loop invariant, a function contract or a patch in seconds. It cannot tell you whether any of those things is actually correct. A model checker can. Unwinding assertions confirm that a loop bound covers every iteration, k-induction proves properties of unbounded executions, and ranking functions prove that loops terminate. The checker still needs a property to verify, and for deep/nested loops and large codebases the proof often depends on an invariant or contract that no one has written. Each side fills a gap in the other.

Since 2023 our Systems and Software Security (S3) group at the University of Manchester and our collaborators have looked at what happens when the two share a loop. Much of this work has used ESBMC, the SMT-based model checker that we develop. ESBMC combines abstract interpretation through interval analysis, model checking through bounded model checking and k-induction, deductive verification through function contracts [1], and SMT solving. A recent survey looks at how it has become the verification backend for LLM-based tools [2].

flowchart LR
    T["Task<br/>program, property,<br/>or requirement"] --> L["LLM proposes<br/>code, patch, invariant,<br/>contract, spec, translation"]
    L --> V{"Formal tool checks<br/>ESBMC,<br/>automated theorem prover"}
    V -- "holds" --> A["Accepted artifact<br/>with a proof or<br/>bounded guarantee"]
    V -- "fails" --> C["Counterexample<br/>trace, line, property"]
    C --> L

Figure 1. The loop shared by most of the papers below. The LLM never makes the correctness decision; the formal tool does.

Our work since 2023

1. How safe is LLM-generated code?

We started off by asking how often LLM-written code is unsafe, and used ESBMC to find out. More than half of the C programs that GPT-3.5-turbo wrote for our FormAI dataset had at least one vulnerability [3], and a follow-up across nine LLMs found at least 62% [4].

Model checking every completion is too slow for an IDE, so we used these verifier-checked labels to train SecureFalcon, a small classifier that flags vulnerable code instantly on a CPU [5].

Formal tools have blind spots too. On the CASTLE benchmark, ESBMC raised the fewest false alarms but missed vulnerabilities outside the properties it checks, such as weak cryptography, while LLMs got worse as programs grew [6]. A survey chapter covers the wider area [7].

2. Counterexample-guided repair and generation

When ESBMC finds a violation, it returns a counterexample: a concrete input and the execution trace that leads to the failing check. That makes it a precise bug report, so we pass it back to an LLM. ESBMC-AI (posted May 2023) takes the source code, the counterexample and the stack trace and feeds it to an LLM, and ESBMC then re-verifies the patch. It was evaluated on 50k FormAI programs [8]. ESBMC-AI has since been succeeded by Entoli, an open-source agent with formal-verification-based workflows. The same loop also works for neural-network code: ESBMC checked about 81k mutated neural-network programs, and an LLM repaired the bugs that ESBMC found [9]. VeriExploit runs it in reverse: you start with a Solidity counterexample and an LLM generates an attacker contract which re-triggers the bug. That contract is then validated by a model checker and is able to reproduce 85.60% of the bugs in our benchmark [10]. For legacy C code, UnitTenX turns ESBMC counterexamples into readable unit tests [11].

3. LLMs supply what the verifier is missing

Here the LLM writes out the invariants and contracts that a proof needs, and a sound tool then decides whether to believe them.

  • Invariants. ESBMC ibmc replaces each loop with an LLM-generated invariant which a theorem prover then checks. It was able to verify programs that SeaHorn and VeriAbs were unable to verify and went on to receive an ACM SIGSOFT Distinguished Paper Award [12]. VerIbmc takes the same approach using open-weight models on a single local machine and solves 431 of the 499 problems in its best configuration, GPT-OSS-120B [13].
  • Contracts. ConVer takes a top-level property and synthesizes function contracts from it, refining them in a CEGAR-CEGIS loop and achieving 82-96% success on 45 Frama-C programs, the easiest of its four benchmark suites, and as low as 33% on the harder ones [14]. For regression verification, partial LLM-inferred contracts produced zero false equivalence proofs on EqBench-C [15].
  • Agents. Agentic model checking is based on the principle of ‘agents propose, solvers verify’ where the agent works out the specifications and plans the run, with all soundness-critical decisions remaining with the bounded model checker (CBMC and Kani). On mature, heavily fuzzed software it found 68 source-audited defects across 11 projects [16].

4. From prose and other languages to checkable models

SpecVerify uses Claude 3.5 Sonnet in conjunction with ESBMC to derive properties from requirements. On nine of Lockheed Martin’s cyber-physical systems it achieved the same result as NASA’s CoCoSim but with fewer false positives [17]. The models still occasionally misread the specifications, so human review remained necessary. INVAR takes a document (e.g. the USB 2.0 or CXL 4.0 specification) and extracts a transition system from it, which it then checks with NuSMV and reports any missing evidence as a named gap rather than a vacuous pass [18]. With NASA JPL we use an LLM to translate Python into C for ESBMC. The paper makes the caveat that as the translation doesn’t prove equivalence the outcome is only bug finding and not verification [19]; the agent and benchmark are both public.

5. Reviews of the field

Two reviews place this work in a wider context: one which provides a taxonomy of the generative transformations and their recurring patterns in over 100 LLM-based proposals for software verification and falsification [20], and one which is a systematic review of 38 studies on LLM agents, which identifies specification as the bottleneck rather than checking [21].

How the pieces fit together

timeline
    2023 : FormAI dataset
         : ESBMC-AI preprint
    2024 : LLM invariants, ESBMC ibmc
         : Repair of neural-network code
    2025 : FormAI-v2, nine LLMs
         : SecureFalcon, CASTLE
         : SpecVerify, VeriExploit, UnitTenX
    2026 : ConVer, VerIbmc, partial contracts
         : Python translation, INVAR
    2027 : Agentic model checking

Figure 2. Timeline by publication year, or by first preprint for ESBMC-AI and for work not yet at a venue.

The papers all follow the same pattern of division of labor. The LLM does the semantic guessing (what a loop maintains, what a function assumes, what a requirement means). A sound tool provides the guarantee. Over time the LLM has been trusted to do more and more. It started off just being measured, then it was used to repair code under a whole-program verifier, then it was used to write parts of the proof and in the agentic model checking work it’s used to plan the entire run. Invariants and contracts are proved before they are used, so a wrong guess is rejected. Assumptions about the environment are different: they are trusted, not checked. If an LLM writes an assumption that rules out every input reaching an assertion, the verifier reports success vacuously. That is why our pipelines check the evidence itself: each LLM-written harness has a seeded-bug twin that must fail, and INVAR reports missing evidence as a gap rather than a pass. A number of the papers are also direct extensions of one another. FormAI provided the evaluation set for ESBMC-AI and the training data for SecureFalcon. VerIbmc builds on the ibmc invariant work.

The negative results are just as important as the positive ones. CASTLE shows us the limitations of the formal tools. SpecVerify shows that the prose still requires a human to read it. The Python work is very clear that, without a verified translation, the method can find bugs but cannot prove the code correct.

Lessons learned

Benchmarks come with an answer key; production code does not. In recent work an LLM agent drafted verification harnesses for codebases such as the AWS SDK for C++, NVIDIA OpenSMA firmware and vLLM, ESBMC checked them, and maintainers merged 18 fixes upstream, including fixes for two CVEs in the AWS SDK for C++. Five lessons from that work and the papers above, presented at FATTW 2026:

  1. Zero false positives beats a higher proof rate. Developers stop trusting a tool that raises false alarms.
  2. Maintainers fix what arrives with a concrete input. The counterexample is the bug report.
  3. The generator’s quality still propagates. With GPT-4o instead of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, SpecVerify produced 8 false positives instead of 0.
  4. We do not win every benchmark. SeaHorn proves more programs than ibmc, and CoCoSim matches SpecVerify; portfolios beat single tools.
  5. Verifiers have traps too. Zero verification conditions, disabled unwinding assertions and contracts that silently check nothing all look like success, so the evidence itself needs checking.

What comes next

There are three challenges that neither academia nor industry can solve alone:

  • Verification at generation speed. Agents generate code in seconds, while industrial proofs take minutes to hours. Faster tools will not close this gap entirely: program verification is undecidable in general (Rice’s theorem), so some checks can end in a timeout or an unknown verdict. Checking must reuse earlier proofs incrementally and report honestly when it cannot decide.
  • Guarantees for agent workflows. Verifying each agent is not enough to verify the workflow they form; we need compositional contracts between agents.
  • Evidence we can trust. DO-178C, the standard for airborne software, already accepts formal evidence through its formal methods supplement, DO-333, which raises the question of who checks the checker. Witnesses and validators are part of the answer.

Underneath all three sits the problem that every line of work above runs into: how do we validate a specification an LLM has derived from natural language before anything is proved against it?

Join us

We’re looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators who are interested in working on these problems (formal methods, program analysis, machine learning etc). Our tools are open source and most of the papers listed above come with the associated artifacts so you can run them. If this is of interest to you then just get in touch with Lucas Cordeiro with a brief note on what you’d like to work on. To talk with the group first, join our public Zulip chat.

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more.
